cleanIntro: A small-frame Colt carry revolver cleans in five minutes and mostly needs it because of where it lives: pocket lint, sweat and holster grit do more damage to a carry gun than shooting does. Six .38 Special chambers, cylinder out to the left, and nothing taken apart.

steps.title: Finger off, muzzle safe, hammer down
steps.action: Keep your finger outside the trigger guard and the muzzle pointed somewhere that would not matter, and make sure the hammer is not cocked before you touch the cylinder latch. A cocked Night Cobra holds the cylinder locked, and forcing the latch against a cocked action is how the hand and the bolt get damaged.

steps.title: Latch REARWARD — this is a Colt, not a Smith or a Ruger
steps.action: Pull the cylinder latch toward the rear of the gun and push the cylinder out to the left. The direction matters and catches people who own other brands: a Smith & Wesson latch pushes forward and a Ruger uses a recessed button, but every Colt double action releases by pulling rearward. If it does not move, the hammer is back.

steps.title: All six chambers empty, by eye and by finger
steps.action: With the cylinder swung out, push the ejector rod to clear the six chambers, then look through every one and run a fingertip across the rear face. A .38 Special case is easy to miss against a dark chamber and impossible to miss by touch. Let the ejector rod return on its own rather than snapping it back.

steps.title: Carry gun: check for lint before solvent
steps.action: Before anything wet touches it, look into the action gap, under the ejector star and around the firing pin hole for pocket lint and holster debris. On a carry revolver that is the most common cause of a heavy trigger or a cylinder that will not quite close, and solvent just turns it into paste.

steps.title: Bore first, from the breech end
steps.action: With the cylinder open you have a clear run at the barrel from the breech end, which is the direction that protects the crown. Solvent on a brush, through and out, then patches until they come out clean. On a .38 Special revolver the last inch ahead of the forcing cone is where fouling collects hardest.

steps.title: Each of the six chambers, individually
steps.action: Chambers are not the bore and a bore brush is the wrong size for them. Use a chamber brush or a patch on a jag, one chamber at a time, and pay attention to the chamber mouths: lead and copper build a ring there, and a fouled mouth is what makes cases stick and extraction stiff.

steps.title: Cylinder face and the barrel's rear face
steps.action: The front face of the cylinder and the rear face of the barrel take the worst of the blast, and the grey ring that builds on both is a real problem rather than a cosmetic one — enough of it and the cylinder gap closes up and the gun binds. A small brush with a little solvent, working outward from the centre.

steps.title: Behind the ejector star — the one everybody skips
steps.action: Push the ejector rod back so the star lifts clear and clean underneath it, then let it seat. Unburnt powder gets under the star and packs solid, and the symptom is a cylinder that will not close fully or a revolver that suddenly will not carry up. Clean the ratchet teeth on the rear face while you are there.

steps.title: Crane, frame window and the ejector rod
steps.action: Wipe the crane where it pivots, the inside of the frame window and the length of the ejector rod. These are bearing surfaces on a revolver and grit here shows up as a gritty double-action pull long before it shows up as a malfunction. Nothing comes apart to do this — a cloth and a small brush reach all of it.

steps.title: Oil like you mean to shoot it, not to store it
steps.action: A thin film on the bore and chambers, a trace on the crane and the ejector rod, and a wipe over the outside with an oiled cloth. Then take the oil back out of the bore and chambers with a dry patch before you shoot: standing oil in a chamber raises pressure and in a bore it just collects the next round of fouling.

steps.title: Two drops inside, through the crane opening
steps.action: The Night Cobra is double-action-only with a bobbed hammer, so there is no hammer to cock and no way to open the internals that way. Put two drops of oil through the crane opening instead, with the cylinder swung out, and work the action slowly a few times to carry it in. Two drops is the whole of it: this revolver rides against a body all day and surplus oil inside the frame collects lint faster than it protects anything.
steps.prose: ⚠ If the revolver in your hand has a hammer spur you can thumb back, it is a Cobra or a King Cobra, not a Night Cobra — and this listing is not the one for it.

steps.title: ⛔ It does not come apart, and that is the whole design
steps.action: This is where an owner stops. Colt's instruction for its modern double-action revolvers is not to field strip them at all — no sideplate, no crane screw, no cylinder off the crane — and anything that needs more than a cylinder-out clean goes to Colt or a competent gunsmith. A revolver's lockwork is a stack of fitted parts under spring load, and the sideplate is the last thing an owner should be prying at.

deepAbsentReason: There is no deep clean for this listing and there should not be one. Colt's published instruction for its modern double-action revolvers is not to field strip them at all — the sideplate, the lockwork, the crane screw and the cylinder assembly are Colt's work or a gunsmith's, and the maker says so in capitals in every current revolver manual it publishes. This row is a best-practices row (ruling 2026-08-20 §2c), which the same ruling caps at basic-clean depth in any case; here the cap and the manufacturer's own limit are the same line.

cleaning.name: BORE
tasks: Brush and solvent from the breech end with the cylinder open
Patches until they come out clean, then a light oiled patch
Dry patch before shooting — no standing oil in the bore

cleaning.name: CHAMBERS (six)
tasks: Chamber brush or a jag and patch, one chamber at a time
Work the chamber mouths — a fouling ring there makes extraction stiff
Light oil, then dry before shooting

cleaning.name: CYLINDER FACES & RATCHET
tasks: Front face of the cylinder and rear face of the barrel — the blast ring
Ejector rod pushed back, clean behind the star and on the ratchet teeth

cleaning.name: CRANE & FRAME
tasks: Crane pivot, frame window and the ejector rod wiped
A trace of oil on the bearing surfaces only
Exterior wiped with a lightly oiled cloth

reassembly: Nothing was taken apart, so there is nothing to put back — that is the point.
Swing the cylinder into the frame and let the latch snap forward on its own; do not flick it closed, which batters the crane and can spring it out of true.
Run a dry patch through the bore and every chamber to take the oil back out before you load.
Function check before any live ammunition.
fncheck: Cylinder closed and latched, chambers proven empty, muzzle safe. Open and close the cylinder several times and feel it drop in and lock without dragging. Then, with the gun still empty, work the action through a full double-action stroke slowly and watch the cylinder carry up and lock before the hammer falls — if it locks late, stop and get it looked at rather than shooting it. Check the cylinder does not rotate freely when the action is at rest. Anything that feels gritty, late or loose goes to Colt or a gunsmith. On a carry gun, finish by checking the cylinder latch is not fouled with lint and that the cylinder locks up with no perceptible rotational play at rest.
